why: hemizygous: the presence of only one allele for a characteristic, as in X-linkage; hemizygosity makes descriptions of dominance and recessiveness irrelevant

q: Which term matches this definition? “in a heterozygote, expression of two contrasting alleles such that the individual displays an intermediate phenotype”
why: incomplete dominance: in a heterozygote, expression of two contrasting alleles such that the individual displays an intermediate phenotype

q: Which term matches this definition? “a phenomenon in which alleles that are located in close proximity to each other on the same chromosome are more likely to be inherited together”
why: linkage: a phenomenon in which alleles that are located in close proximity to each other on the same chromosome are more likely to be inherited together

q: Which term matches this definition? “the process during meiosis in which homologous chromosomes exchange linear segments of genetic material, thereby dramatically increasing genetic variation in the offspring and separating linked genes”
why: recombination: the process during meiosis in which homologous chromosomes exchange linear segments of genetic material, thereby dramatically increasing genetic variation in the offspring and separating linked genes

card.q: What ratio of offspring would result from a cross between a white-eyed male and a female that is heterozygous for red eye color?
card.a: Half of the female offspring would be heterozygous (X^WX^w) with red eyes, and half would be homozygous recessive (X^wX^w) with white eyes. Half of the male offspring would be hemizygous dominant (X^WY) with red eyes, and half would be hemizygous recessive (X^wY) with white eyes.

card.q: Can a male be a carrier of red-green color blindness?
card.a: No, males can only express color blindness and cannot carry it because an individual needs two X chromosomes to be a carrier.

card.q: Could an individual with blood type O (genotype ii) be a legitimate child of parents in which one parent had blood type A and the other parent had blood type B?
card.a: Yes this child could have come from these parents. The child would have inherited an i allele from each parent and for this to happen the type A parent had to have genotype I^Ai and the type b parent had to have genotype I^Bi.

q: Which of the following does cytosine pair with?
why: The correct answer is: guanine. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Prokaryotes contain a ________chromosome, and eukaryotes contain ________ chromosomes.
why: The correct answer is: double-stranded circular; double-stranded linear. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a five-carbon sugar molecule with a hydrogen atom rather than a hydroxyl group in the 2' position; the sugar component of DNA nucleotides”
why: deoxyribose: a five-carbon sugar molecule with a hydrogen atom rather than a hydroxyl group in the 2' position; the sugar component of DNA nucleotides

q: Which term matches this definition? “the molecular shape of DNA in which two strands of nucleotides wind around each other in a spiral shape”
why: double helix: the molecular shape of DNA in which two strands of nucleotides wind around each other in a spiral shape

q: Which term matches this definition? “a nitrogen-containing molecule that acts as a base; often referring to one of the purine or pyrimidine components of nucleic acids”
why: nitrogenous base: a nitrogen-containing molecule that acts as a base; often referring to one of the purine or pyrimidine components of nucleic acids

q: Which term matches this definition? “a molecular group consisting of a central phosphorus atom bound to four oxygen atoms”
why: phosphate group: a molecular group consisting of a central phosphorus atom bound to four oxygen atoms

card.q: Describe the organization of the eukaryotic chromosome.
card.a: The DNA is wound around proteins called histones. The histones then stack together in a compact form that creates a fiber that is 30-nm thick. The fiber is further coiled for greater compactness. During metaphase of mitosis, the chromosome is at its most compact to facilitate chromosome movement. During interphase, there are denser areas of chromatin, called heterochromatin, that contain DNA that is not expressed, and less dense euchromatin that contains DNA that is expressed.

card.q: Describe the structure and complementary base pairing of DNA.
card.a: A single strand of DNA is a polymer of nucleic acids joined covalently between the phosphate group of one and the deoxyribose sugar of the next to for a “backbone” from which the nitrogenous bases stick out. In its natural state, DNA has two strands wound around each other in a double helix. The bases on each strand are bonded to each other with hydrogen bonds. Only specific bases bond with each other; adenine bonds with thymine, and cytosine bonds with guanine.

q: DNA replicates by which of the following models?
why: The correct answer is: semiconservative. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The initial mechanism for repairing nucleotide errors in DNA is ________.
why: The correct answer is: DNA polymerase proofreading. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the enzyme that catalyzes the joining of DNA fragments together”
why: DNA ligase: the enzyme that catalyzes the joining of DNA fragments together

q: Which term matches this definition? “an enzyme that synthesizes a new strand of DNA complementary to a template strand”
why: DNA polymerase: an enzyme that synthesizes a new strand of DNA complementary to a template strand

q: Which term matches this definition? “an enzyme that helps to open up the DNA helix during DNA replication by breaking the hydrogen bonds”
why: helicase: an enzyme that helps to open up the DNA helix during DNA replication by breaking the hydrogen bonds

q: Which term matches this definition? “during replication of the 3' to 5' strand, the strand that is replicated in short fragments and away from the replication fork”
why: lagging strand: during replication of the 3' to 5' strand, the strand that is replicated in short fragments and away from the replication fork

q: Which term matches this definition? “the strand that is synthesized continuously in the 5' to 3' direction that is synthesized in the direction of the replication fork”
why: leading strand: the strand that is synthesized continuously in the 5' to 3' direction that is synthesized in the direction of the replication fork

q: Which term matches this definition? “a form of DNA repair in which non-complementary nucleotides are recognized, excised, and replaced with correct nucleotides”
why: mismatch repair: a form of DNA repair in which non-complementary nucleotides are recognized, excised, and replaced with correct nucleotides

card.q: You isolate a cell strain in which the joining together of Okazaki fragments is impaired and suspect that a mutation has occurred in an enzyme found at the replication fork. Which enzyme is most likely to be mutated?
card.a: Ligase, as this enzyme joins together Okazaki fragments.

card.q: How do the linear chromosomes in eukaryotes ensure that its ends are replicated completely?
card.a: Telomerase has an inbuilt RNA template that extends the 3' end, so a primer is synthesized and extended. Thus, the ends are protected.

q: A promoter is ________.
options: a specific sequence of DNA nucleotides
a specific sequence of RNA nucleotides
a protein that binds to DNA
why: The correct answer is: a specific sequence of DNA nucleotides. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Portions of eukaryotic mRNA sequence that are removed during RNA processing are ________.
why: The correct answer is: introns. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a sequence present in protein-coding mRNA after completion of pre-mRNA splicing”
why: exon: a sequence present in protein-coding mRNA after completion of pre-mRNA splicing

q: Which term matches this definition? “non–protein-coding intervening sequences that are spliced from mRNA during processing”
why: intron: non–protein-coding intervening sequences that are spliced from mRNA during processing

q: Which term matches this definition? “messenger RNA; a form of RNA that carries the nucleotide sequence code for a protein sequence that is translated into a polypeptide sequence”
why: mRNA: messenger RNA; a form of RNA that carries the nucleotide sequence code for a protein sequence that is translated into a polypeptide sequence

q: Which term matches this definition? “the strand of DNA that is not used to transcribe mRNA; this strand is identical to the mRNA except that T nucleotides in the DNA are replaced by U nucleotides in the mRNA”
why: nontemplate strand: the strand of DNA that is not used to transcribe mRNA; this strand is identical to the mRNA except that T nucleotides in the DNA are replaced by U nucleotides in the mRNA

q: Which term matches this definition? “a sequence on DNA to which RNA polymerase and associated factors bind and initiate transcription”
why: promoter: a sequence on DNA to which RNA polymerase and associated factors bind and initiate transcription

q: Which term matches this definition? “an enzyme that synthesizes an RNA strand from a DNA template strand”
why: RNA polymerase: an enzyme that synthesizes an RNA strand from a DNA template strand

q: The RNA components of ribosomes are synthesized in the ________.
why: The correct answer is: nucleolus. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: How long would the peptide be that is translated from this MRNA sequence: 5'-AUGGGCUACCGA-3'?
why: The correct answer is: 4. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “three consecutive nucleotides in mRNA that specify the addition of a specific amino acid or the release of a polypeptide chain during translation”
why: codon: three consecutive nucleotides in mRNA that specify the addition of a specific amino acid or the release of a polypeptide chain during translation

q: Which term matches this definition? “the amino acids that correspond to three-nucleotide codons of mRNA”
why: genetic code: the amino acids that correspond to three-nucleotide codons of mRNA

q: Which term matches this definition? “ribosomal RNA; molecules of RNA that combine to form part of the ribosome”
why: rRNA: ribosomal RNA; molecules of RNA that combine to form part of the ribosome

q: Which term matches this definition? “one of the three mRNA codons that specifies termination of translation”
why: stop codon: one of the three mRNA codons that specifies termination of translation

q: Which term matches this definition? “the AUG (or, rarely GUG) on an mRNA from which translation begins; always specifies methionine”
why: start codon: the AUG (or, rarely GUG) on an mRNA from which translation begins; always specifies methionine

q: Which term matches this definition? “transfer RNA; an RNA molecule that contains a specific three-nucleotide anticodon sequence to pair with the mRNA codon and also binds to a specific amino acid”
why: tRNA: transfer RNA; an RNA molecule that contains a specific three-nucleotide anticodon sequence to pair with the mRNA codon and also binds to a specific amino acid

card.q: Transcribe and translate the following DNA sequence (nontemplate strand): 5'-ATGGCCGGTTATTAAGCA-3'
card.a: The mRNA would be: 5'-AUGGCCGGUUAUUAAGCA-3'. The protein would be: MAGY. Even though there are six codons, the fifth codon corresponds to a stop, so the sixth codon would not be translated.

q: Control of gene expression in eukaryotic cells occurs at which level(s)?
options: epigenetic, transcriptional, post-transcriptional, translational, and post-translational levels
why: The correct answer is: epigenetic, transcriptional, post-transcriptional, translational, and post-translational levels. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Post-translational control refers to:
options: regulation of gene expression after transcription
regulation of gene expression after translation
why: The correct answer is: regulation of gene expression after translation. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a post-transcriptional gene regulation mechanism in eukaryotes in which multiple protein products are produced by a single gene through alternative splicing combinations of the RNA transcript”
why: alternative RNA splicing: a post-transcriptional gene regulation mechanism in eukaryotes in which multiple protein products are produced by a single gene through alternative splicing combinations of the RNA transcript

q: Which term matches this definition? “describing non-genetic regulatory factors, such as changes in modifications to histone proteins and DNA that control accessibility to genes in chromosomes”
why: epigenetic: describing non-genetic regulatory factors, such as changes in modifications to histone proteins and DNA that control accessibility to genes in chromosomes

q: Which term matches this definition? “processes that control whether a gene is expressed”
why: gene expression: processes that control whether a gene is expressed

q: Which term matches this definition? “control of gene expression after the RNA molecule has been created but before it is translated into protein”
why: post-transcriptional: control of gene expression after the RNA molecule has been created but before it is translated into protein

q: Which term matches this definition? “control of gene expression after a protein has been created”
why: post-translational: control of gene expression after a protein has been created

card.q: Describe how controlling gene expression will alter the overall protein levels in the cell.
card.a: The cell controls which protein is expressed, and to what level that protein is expressed, in the cell. Prokaryotic cells alter the transcription rate to turn genes on or off. This method will increase or decrease protein levels in response to what is needed by the cell. Eukaryotic cells change the accessibility (epigenetic), transcription, or translation of a gene. This will alter the amount of RNA, and the lifespan of the RNA, to alter the amount of protein that exists. Eukaryotic cells also change the protein’s translation to increase or decrease its overall levels. Eukaryotic organisms are much more complex and can manipulate protein levels by changing many stages in the process.

q: In gel electrophoresis of DNA, the different bands in the final gel form because the DNA molecules ________.
why: The correct answer is: have different lengths. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In the reproductive cloning of an animal, the genome of the cloned individual comes from ________.
why: The correct answer is: a body cell. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What carries a gene from one organism into a bacteria cell?
why: The correct answer is: a plasmid. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “in molecular biology, the process by which two single strands of DNA hydrogen bond at complementary nucleotides to form a double-stranded molecule”
why: anneal: in molecular biology, the process by which two single strands of DNA hydrogen bond at complementary nucleotides to form a double-stranded molecule

q: Which term matches this definition? “the use of artificial methods to modify the genetic material of living organisms or cells to produce novel compounds or to perform new functions”
why: biotechnology: the use of artificial methods to modify the genetic material of living organisms or cells to produce novel compounds or to perform new functions

q: Which term matches this definition? “the production of an exact copy—specifically, an exact genetic copy—of a gene, cell, or organism”
why: cloning: the production of an exact copy—specifically, an exact genetic copy—of a gene, cell, or organism

q: Which term matches this definition? “a technique used to separate molecules on the basis of their ability to migrate through a semisolid gel in response to an electric current”
why: gel electrophoresis: a technique used to separate molecules on the basis of their ability to migrate through a semisolid gel in response to an electric current

q: Which term matches this definition? “alteration of the genetic makeup of an organism using the molecular methods of biotechnology”
why: genetic engineering: alteration of the genetic makeup of an organism using the molecular methods of biotechnology

q: Which term matches this definition? “an organism whose genome has been artificially changed”
why: genetically modified organism (GMO): an organism whose genome has been artificially changed

card.q: Why was Dolly a Finn-Dorset and not a Scottish Blackface sheep?
card.a: Because even though the original cell came from a Scottish Blackface sheep and the surrogate mother was a Scottish Blackface, the DNA came from a Finn-Dorset.

card.q: What is the purpose and benefit of the polymerase chain reaction?
card.a: The polymerase chain reaction is used to quickly produce many copies of a specific segment of DNA when only one or a very few copies are originally present. The benefit of PCR is that there are many instances in which we would like to know something about a sample of DNA when only very small amounts are available. PCR allows us to increase the number of DNA molecules so that other tests, such as sequencing, can be performed with it.

q: What is a genetically modified organism (GMO)?
options: a plant with certain genes removed
an organism with an artificially altered genome
any agricultural organism produced by breeding or biotechnology
why: The correct answer is: an organism with an artificially altered genome. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the role of Agrobacterium tumefaciens in the production of transgenic plants?
options: Genes from A. tumefaciens are inserted into plant DNA to give the plant different traits.
Transgenic plants have been given resistance to the pest A. tumefaciens.
A. tumefaciens is used as a vector to move genes into plant cells.
Plant genes are incorporated into the genome of Agrobacterium tumefaciens.
why: The correct answer is: A. tumefaciens is used as a vector to move genes into plant cells.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the technique used to cure heritable diseases by replacing mutant genes with good genes”
why: gene therapy: the technique used to cure heritable diseases by replacing mutant genes with good genes

q: Which term matches this definition? “identifying gene variants in an individual that may lead to a genetic disease in that individual”
why: genetic testing: identifying gene variants in an individual that may lead to a genetic disease in that individual

card.q: Today, it is possible for a diabetic patient to purchase human insulin from a pharmacist. What technology makes this possible and why is it a benefit over how things used to be?
card.a: The human insulin comes from the gene that produces insulin in humans, which has been spliced into a bacterial genome using recombinant DNA technology. The bacterium produces the insulin, which is then purified for human use. Before there was genetically engineered human insulin, diabetics were given insulin extracted from pig pancreases, which was similar to, but not exactly like, human insulin. Because it was not exactly like human insulin, the pig insulin caused complications in some diabetic patients.

q: What is the most challenging issue facing genome sequencing?
options: the inability to develop fast and accurate sequencing techniques
the ethics of using information from genomes at the individual level
the availability and stability of DNA
why: The correct answer is: the ethics of using information from genomes at the individual level. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Genomics can be used in agriculture to:
why: The correct answer is: all of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What kind of diseases are studied using genome-wide association studies?
why: The correct answer is: diseases caused by multiple genes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “an individual protein that is uniquely produced in a diseased state”
why: biomarker: an individual protein that is uniquely produced in a diseased state

q: Which term matches this definition? “an outline of genes and their location on a chromosome that is based on recombination frequencies between markers”
why: genetic map: an outline of genes and their location on a chromosome that is based on recombination frequencies between markers

q: Which term matches this definition? “the study of entire genomes, including the complete set of genes, their nucleotide sequence and organization, and their interactions within a species and with other species”
why: genomics: the study of entire genomes, including the complete set of genes, their nucleotide sequence and organization, and their interactions within a species and with other species

q: Which term matches this definition? “the study of the collective genomes of multiple species that grow and interact in an environmental niche”
why: metagenomics: the study of the collective genomes of multiple species that grow and interact in an environmental niche

q: Which term matches this definition? “a species that is studied and used as a model to understand the biological processes in other species represented by the model organism”
why: model organism: a species that is studied and used as a model to understand the biological processes in other species represented by the model organism

q: Which term matches this definition? “the study of drug interactions with the genome or proteome; also called toxicogenomics”
why: pharmacogenomics: the study of drug interactions with the genome or proteome; also called toxicogenomics

card.q: Describe two of the applications for genome mapping.
card.a: Genome mapping helps researchers to study disease-causing genes in humans. It also helps to identify traits of organisms that can be used in applications such as cleaning up pollution.

card.q: Identify a possible advantage and a possible disadvantage of a genetic test that would identify genes in individuals that increase their probability of having Alzheimer's disease later in life.
card.a: The benefit of such a test is that the individual can make preparations for having the disease including taking treatments that slow the disease. The disadvantage of the test is that it might be used by insurance companies to deny coverage to the person.

q: Which scientific concept did Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace independently discover?
why: The correct answer is: natural selection. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following situations will lead to natural selection?
options: The seeds of two plants land near each other and one grows larger than the other.
Two types of fish eat the same kind of food, and one is better able to gather food than the other.
Male lions compete for the right to mate with females, with only one possible winner.
why: The correct answer is: all of the above. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the difference between micro- and macroevolution?
options: Microevolution describes the evolution of small organisms, such as insects, while macroevolution describes the evolution of large organisms, like people and elephants.
Microevolution describes the evolution of microscopic entities, such as molecules and proteins, while macroevolution describes the evolution of whole organisms.
Microevolution describes the evolution of populations, while macroevolution describes the emergence of new species over long periods of time.
Microevolution describes the evolution of organisms over their lifetimes, while macroevolution describes the evolution of organisms over multiple generations.
why: The correct answer is: Microevolution describes the evolution of populations, while macroevolution describes the emergence of new species over long periods of time.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Population genetics is the study of ________.
options: how allele frequencies in a population change over time
populations of cells in an individual
why: The correct answer is: how allele frequencies in a population change over time. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a heritable trait or behavior in an organism that aids in its survival in its present environment”
why: adaptation: a heritable trait or behavior in an organism that aids in its survival in its present environment

q: Which term matches this definition? “a structure that is similar because of evolution in response to similar selection pressures resulting in convergent evolution, not similar because of descent from a common ancestor”
why: analogous structure: a structure that is similar because of evolution in response to similar selection pressures resulting in convergent evolution, not similar because of descent from a common ancestor

q: Which term matches this definition? “an evolution that results in similar forms on different species”
why: convergent evolution: an evolution that results in similar forms on different species

q: Which term matches this definition? “an evolution that results in different forms in two species with a common ancestor”
why: divergent evolution: an evolution that results in different forms in two species with a common ancestor

q: Which term matches this definition? “all of the alleles carried by all of the individuals in the population”
why: gene pool: all of the alleles carried by all of the individuals in the population

q: Which term matches this definition? “the effect of chance on a population’s gene pool”
why: genetic drift: the effect of chance on a population’s gene pool

card.q: If a person scatters a handful of plant seeds from one species in an area, how would natural selection work in this situation?
card.a: The plants that can best use the resources of the area, including competing with other individuals for those resources, will produce more seeds themselves and those traits that allowed them to better use the resources will increase in the population of the next generation.

card.q: Explain the Hardy-Weinberg principle of equilibrium.
card.a: The Hardy-Weinberg principle of equilibrium states that a population’s allele frequencies are inherently stable. Unless an evolutionary force is acting upon the population, the population would carry the same genes at the same frequencies generation after generation, and individuals would, as a whole, look essentially the same.

q: Galápagos medium ground finches are found on Santa Cruz and San Cristóbal islands, which are separated by about 100 km of ocean. Occasionally, individuals from either island fly to the other island to stay. This can alter the allele frequencies of the population through which of the following mechanisms?
why: The correct answer is: gene flow. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: In which of the following pairs do both evolutionary processes introduce new genetic variation into a population?
why: The correct answer is: mutation and gene flow. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the magnification of genetic drift as a result of natural events or catastrophes”
why: bottleneck effect: the magnification of genetic drift as a result of natural events or catastrophes

q: Which term matches this definition? “a magnification of genetic drift in a small population that migrates away from a large parent population carrying with it an unrepresentative set of alleles”
why: founder effect: a magnification of genetic drift in a small population that migrates away from a large parent population carrying with it an unrepresentative set of alleles

q: Which term matches this definition? “the flow of alleles in and out of a population due to the migration of individuals or gametes”
why: gene flow: the flow of alleles in and out of a population due to the migration of individuals or gametes

card.q: Do you think genetic drift would happen more quickly on an island or on the mainland?
card.a: Genetic drift is likely to occur more rapidly on an island, where smaller populations are expected to occur.

card.q: Describe natural selection and give an example of natural selection at work in a population.
card.a: The theory of natural selection stems from the observation that some individuals in a population survive longer and have more offspring than others, thus passing on more of their genes to the next generation. For example, a big, powerful male gorilla is much more likely than a smaller, weaker gorilla to become the population’s silverback, the pack’s leader who mates far more than the other males of the group. The pack leader will, therefore, father more offspring, who share half of his genes, and are thus likely to also grow bigger and stronger like their father. Over time, the genes for bigger size will increase in frequency in the population, and the population will, as a result, grow larger on average.

q: The wing of a bird and the arm of a human are examples of ________.
why: The correct answer is: homologous structures. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The fact that DNA sequences are more similar in more closely related organisms is evidence of what?
why: The correct answer is: descent with modification. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a physical structure present in an organism but that has no apparent function and appears to be from a functional structure in a distant ancestor”
why: vestigial structure: a physical structure present in an organism but that has no apparent function and appears to be from a functional structure in a distant ancestor

card.q: Why do scientists consider vestigial structures evidence for evolution?
card.a: A vestigial structure is an example of a homologous structure that has apparently been reduced through evolution to a non-functional state because its function is no longer utilized by the species exhibiting it; therefore, any mutations which might reduce its structure are not selected against. The fact that the species has vestiges of the structure rather than no structure at all is evidence that it was present in an ancestor and evolved to non-functionality through accumulation of random mutations.

q: Which situation would most likely lead to allopatric speciation?
options: A flood causes the formation of a new lake.
A storm causes several large trees to fall down.
A mutation causes a new trait to develop.
An injury causes an organism to seek out a new food source.
why: The correct answer is: A flood causes the formation of a new lake.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is the main difference between dispersal and vicariance?
options: One leads to allopatric speciation, whereas the other leads to sympatric speciation.
One involves the movement of the organism, whereas the other involves a change in the environment.
One depends on a genetic mutation occurring, whereas the other does not.
One involves closely related organisms, whereas the other involves only individuals of the same species.
why: The correct answer is: One involves the movement of the organism, whereas the other involves a change in the environment.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which variable increases the likelihood of allopatric speciation taking place more quickly?
options: equivalent numbers of individuals in each population
why: The correct answer is: longer distance between divided groups. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a speciation when one species radiates out to form several other species”
why: adaptive radiation: a speciation when one species radiates out to form several other species

q: Which term matches this definition? “a speciation that occurs via a geographic separation”
why: allopatric speciation: a speciation that occurs via a geographic separation

q: Which term matches this definition? “an allopatric speciation that occurs when a few members of a species move to a new geographical area”
why: dispersal: an allopatric speciation that occurs when a few members of a species move to a new geographical area

q: Which term matches this definition? “a formation of a new species”
why: speciation: a formation of a new species

q: Which term matches this definition? “a speciation that occurs in the same geographic space”
why: sympatric speciation: a speciation that occurs in the same geographic space

q: Which term matches this definition? “an allopatric speciation that occurs when something in the environment separates organisms of the same species into separate groups”
why: vicariance: an allopatric speciation that occurs when something in the environment separates organisms of the same species into separate groups

card.q: Why do island chains provide ideal conditions for adaptive radiation to occur?
card.a: Organisms of one species can arrive to an island together and then disperse throughout the chain, each settling into different niches, exploiting different food resources and, evolving independently with little gene flow between different islands.

card.q: Two species of fish had recently undergone sympatric speciation. The males of each species had a different coloring through which females could identify and choose a partner from her own species. After some time, pollution made the lake so cloudy it was hard for females to distinguish colors. What might take place in this situation?
card.a: It is likely the two species would start to reproduce with each other if hybridization is still possible. Depending on the viability of their offspring, they may fuse back into one species.

q: The word “theory” in theory of evolution is best replaced by ________.
why: The correct answer is: fact. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Why are alternative scientific theories to evolution not taught in public school?
options: there are no viable scientific alternatives
alternative scientific theories are suppressed by the science establishment
why: The correct answer is: there are no viable scientific alternatives. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: How does the scientific meaning of “theory” differ from the common, everyday meaning of the word?
card.a: In science, a theory is a thoroughly tested and verified set of explanations for a body of observations of nature. It is the strongest form of knowledge in science. In contrast, a theory in common usage can mean a guess or speculation about something, meaning that the knowledge implied by the theory may be very weak.

card.q: Explain why the statement that a monkey is more evolved than a mouse is incorrect.
card.a: The statement implies that there is a goal to evolution and that the monkey represents greater progress to that goal than the mouse. Both species are likely to be well adapted to their particular environment, which is the outcome of natural selection.

q: What is a phylogeny a description of?
why: The correct answer is: evolutionary history. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What do scientists in the field of systematics accomplish?
why: The correct answer is: organize and classify organisms. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which statement about the taxonomic classification system is correct?
options: There are more domains than kingdoms.
Kingdoms are the top category of classification.
A phylum may be represented in more than one kingdom.
Species are the most specific category of classification.
why: The correct answer is: Species are the most specific category of classification.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which best describes the relationship between chimpanzees and humans?
options: chimpanzees and humans evolved from a common ancestor
chimpanzees and humans belong to the same species
why: The correct answer is: chimpanzees and humans evolved from a common ancestor. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which best describes a branch point in a phylogenetic tree?
why: The correct answer is: new lineage. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: In what levels are cats and dogs considered to be part of the same group?
card.a: Cats and dogs are part of the same group at five levels: both are in the domain Eukarya, the kingdom Animalia, the phylum Chordata, the class Mammalia, and the order Carnivora.

card.q: How does a phylogenetic tree indicate major evolutionary events within a lineage?
card.a: The phylogenetic tree shows the order in which evolutionary events took place and in what order certain characteristics and organisms evolved in relation to others. It does not generally indicate time durations.

card.q: List the different levels of the taxonomic classification system.
card.a: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, and Species.

q: Which statement about analogies is correct?
options: They are synonymous with homologous traits.
They are derived by response to similar environmental pressures.
They are a form of mutation.
why: The correct answer is: They are derived by response to similar environmental pressures.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What kind of trait is important to cladistics?
why: The correct answer is: shared derived traits. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What is true about organisms that are a part of the same clade?
options: They all share the same basic characteristics.
They evolved from a shared ancestor.
They all are on the same tree.
why: The correct answer is: They evolved from a shared ancestor.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which assumption of cladistics is stated incorrectly?
options: Living things are related by descent from a common ancestor.
Speciation can produce one, two, or three new species.
Traits change from one state to another.
The polarity of a character state change can be determined.
why: The correct answer is: Speciation can produce one, two, or three new species.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: A monophyletic group is a ________.
why: The correct answer is: clade. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Which animals in this figure belong to a clade that includes animals with hair? Which evolved first: hair or the amniotic egg?
card.a: Rabbits and humans belong in the clade that includes animals with hair. The amniotic egg evolved before hair, because the Amniota clade branches off earlier than the clade that encompasses animals with hair.

card.q: Dolphins and fish have similar body shapes. Is this feature more likely a homologous or analogous trait?
card.a: Dolphins are mammals and fish are not, which means that their evolutionary paths (phylogenies) are quite separate. Dolphins probably adapted to have a similar body plan after returning to an aquatic lifestyle, and therefore this trait is probably analogous.

card.q: Describe maximum parsimony.
card.a: Maximum parsimony hypothesizes that events occurred in the simplest, most obvious way, and the pathway of evolution probably includes the fewest major events that coincide with the evidence at hand.

card.q: How does a biologist determine the polarity of a character change?
card.a: The biologist looks at the state of the character in an outgroup, an organism that is outside the clade for which the phylogeny is being developed. The polarity of the character change is from the state of the character in the outgroup to the second state.

q: The first forms of life on Earth were thought to be_______.
why: The correct answer is: prokaryotes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The first organisms that oxygenated the atmosphere were _______.
why: The correct answer is: cyanobacteria. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following consist of prokaryotic cells?
why: The correct answer is: bacteria and archaea. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Prokaryotes stain as Gram-positive or Gram-negative because of differences in the _______.
why: The correct answer is: cell wall. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Prokaryotes that obtain their energy from chemical compounds are called _____.
why: The correct answer is: chemotrophs. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Bioremediation includes _____.
options: the use of prokaryotes that can fix nitrogen
the use of prokaryotes to clean up pollutants
the use of prokaryotes as natural fertilizers
why: The correct answer is: the use of prokaryotes to clean up pollutants. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

card.q: Explain the reason why the imprudent and excessive use of antibiotics has resulted in a major global problem.
card.a: Antibiotics kill bacteria that are sensitive to them; thus, only the resistant ones will survive. These resistant bacteria will reproduce, and therefore, after a while, there will be only resistant bacteria, making it more difficult to treat the diseases they may cause in humans.

card.q: Your friend believes that prokaryotes are always detrimental and pathogenic. How would you explain to them that they are wrong?
card.a: Remind them of the important roles prokaryotes play in decomposition and freeing up nutrients in biogeochemical cycles; remind them of the many prokaryotes that are not human pathogens and that fill very specialized niches.

q: What event is thought to have contributed to the evolution of eukaryotes?
why: The correct answer is: oxygenation of the atmosphere. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Mitochondria most likely evolved from _____________.
why: The correct answer is: aerobic bacteria. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the engulfment of one cell by another such that the engulfed cell survives and both cells benefit; the process responsible for the evolution of mitochondria and chloroplasts in eukaryotes”
why: endosymbiosis: the engulfment of one cell by another such that the engulfed cell survives and both cells benefit; the process responsible for the evolution of mitochondria and chloroplasts in eukaryotes

q: Which term matches this definition? “one of a group of related organelles in plant cells that are involved in the storage of starches, fats, proteins, and pigments”
why: plastid: one of a group of related organelles in plant cells that are involved in the storage of starches, fats, proteins, and pigments

card.q: Describe the hypothesized steps in the origin of eukaryote cells.
card.a: Eukaryote cells arose through endosymbiotic events that gave rise to energy-producing organelles within the eukaryotic cells, such as mitochondria and plastids. The nuclear genome of eukaryotes is related most closely to the Archaea, so it may have been an early archaean that engulfed a bacterial cell that evolved into a mitochondrion. Mitochondria appear to have originated from an alpha-proteobacterium, whereas chloroplasts originated from a cyanobacterium. There is also evidence of secondary endosymbiotic events. Other cell components may have resulted from endosymbiotic events.

q: Protists with the capabilities to absorb nutrients from dead organisms are called_____________.
why: The correct answer is: saprobes. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which parasitic protist evades the host immune system by altering its surface proteins with each generation?
why: The correct answer is: Trypanosoma brucei. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

why: Amoebozoa: the eukaryotic supergroup that contains the amoebas and slime molds

q: Which term matches this definition? “the eukaryotic supergroup that contains land plants, green algae, and red algae”
why: Archaeplastida: the eukaryotic supergroup that contains land plants, green algae, and red algae

q: Which term matches this definition? “the eukaryotic supergroup that contains the dinoflagellates, ciliates, the brown algae, diatoms, and water molds”
why: Chromalveolata: the eukaryotic supergroup that contains the dinoflagellates, ciliates, the brown algae, diatoms, and water molds

q: Which term matches this definition? “the eukaryotic supergroup that contains flagellated single-celled organisms with a feeding groove”
why: Excavata: the eukaryotic supergroup that contains flagellated single-celled organisms with a feeding groove

q: Which term matches this definition? “the eukaryotic supergroup that contains the fungi, animals, and choanoflagellates”
why: Opisthokonta: the eukaryotic supergroup that contains the fungi, animals, and choanoflagellates

q: Which term matches this definition? “an organism that lives on or in another organism and feeds on it, often without killing it”
why: parasite: an organism that lives on or in another organism and feeds on it, often without killing it

card.q: How does killing Anopheles mosquitoes affect the Plasmodium protists?
card.a: Plasmodium parasites infect humans and cause malaria. However, they must complete part of their life cycle within Anopheles mosquitoes, and they can only be transmitted to humans via the bite wound of a mosquito. If the mosquito population were decreased, then fewer Plasmodium would be able to develop and be transmitted to humans, thereby reducing the incidence of human infections with this parasite.

card.q: Without treatment, why does African sleeping sickness invariably lead to death?
card.a: The trypanosomes that cause this disease are capable of expressing a glycoprotein coat with a different molecular structure with each generation. Because the immune system must respond to specific antigens to raise a meaningful defense, the changing nature of trypanosome antigens prevents the immune system from ever clearing this infection. Massive trypanosome infection eventually leads to host organ failure and death.

why: The correct answer is: chitin. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What term describes the close association of a fungus with the root of a tree?
why: The correct answer is: a mycorrhiza. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

why: Chytridiomycota: (chytrids) a primitive division of fungi that live in water and produce gametes with flagella

q: Which term matches this definition? “a group of fungi that form symbiotic relationships with the roots of trees”
why: Glomeromycota: a group of fungi that form symbiotic relationships with the roots of trees

q: Which term matches this definition? “a fungal filament composed of one or more cells”
why: hypha: a fungal filament composed of one or more cells

q: Which term matches this definition? “the close association of a fungus with a photosynthetic alga or bacterium that benefits both partners”
why: lichen: the close association of a fungus with a photosynthetic alga or bacterium that benefits both partners

card.q: Why can superficial mycoses in humans lead to bacterial infections?
card.a: Dermatophytes that colonize skin break down the keratinized layer of dead cells that protects tissues from bacterial invasion. Once the integrity of the skin is breached, bacteria can enter the deeper layers of tissues and cause infections.

why: The correct answer is: green algae. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: The event that leads from the haploid stage to the diploid stage in alternation of generations is ________.
why: The correct answer is: fertilization. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Moss is an example of which type of plant?
why: The correct answer is: haplontic plant. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the growing point in a vascular plant at the tip of a shoot or root where cell division occurs”
why: apical meristem: the growing point in a vascular plant at the tip of a shoot or root where cell division occurs

q: Which term matches this definition? “describes a life cycle in which the diploid stage is the dominant stage”

why: gametangium: (plural: gametangia) the structure within which gametes are produced

q: Which term matches this definition? “the haploid plant that produces gametes”
why: gametophyte: the haploid plant that produces gametes

q: Which term matches this definition? “describes a life cycle in which the haploid and diploid stages alternate; also known as an alternation of generations life cycle”
why: haplodiplontic: describes a life cycle in which the haploid and diploid stages alternate; also known as an alternation of generations life cycle

q: Which term matches this definition? “describes a life cycle in which the haploid stage is the dominant stage”
why: haplontic: describes a life cycle in which the haploid stage is the dominant stage

card.q: What adaptations do plants have that allow them to survive on land?
card.a: The sporangium of plants protects the spores from drying out. Apical meristems ensure that a plant is able to grow in the two directions required to acquire water and nutrients: up toward sunlight and down into the soil. The multicellular embryo is an important adaptation that improves survival of the developing plant in dry environments. The development of molecules that gave plants structural strength allowed them to grow higher on land and obtain more sunlight. A waxy cuticle prevents water loss from aerial surfaces.

q: Why do mosses grow well in the Arctic tundra?
options: They grow better at cold temperatures.
They do not have true roots and can grow on hard surfaces.
There are no herbivores in the tundra.
why: The correct answer is: They do not have true roots and can grow on hard surfaces.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which is the most diverse group of seedless vascular plants?
why: The correct answer is: the ferns. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which group are vascular plants?
why: The correct answer is: ferns. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the earliest group of seedless vascular plants”
why: club moss: the earliest group of seedless vascular plants

q: Which term matches this definition? “a seedless vascular plant that produces large fronds; the most advanced group of seedless vascular plants”

why: horsetail: a seedless vascular plant characterized by a jointed stem

q: Which term matches this definition? “the most primitive group of non-vascular plants”

q: Which term matches this definition? “a group of plants in which a primitive conductive system appears”

card.q: What are the three classes of bryophytes?
card.a: The bryophytes are divided into three divisions: the liverworts or Marchantiophyta, the hornworts or Anthocerotophyta, and the mosses or true Bryophyta.

card.q: How did the development of a vascular system contribute to the increase in size of plants?
card.a: It became possible to transport water and nutrients through the plant and not be limited by rates of diffusion. Vascularization allowed the development of leaves, which increased efficiency of photosynthesis and provided more energy for plant growth.

q: Which of the following traits characterizes gymnosperms?
options: The plants carry exposed seeds on modified leaves.
Reproductive structures are located in a flower.
After fertilization, the ovary thickens and forms a fruit.
The gametophyte is longest phase of the life cycle.
why: The correct answer is: The plants carry exposed seeds on modified leaves.. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: What adaptation do seed plants have in addition to the seed that is not found in seedless plants?
why: The correct answer is: pollen. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “the ovulate strobilus on gymnosperms that contains ovules”
why: cone: the ovulate strobilus on gymnosperms that contains ovules

q: Which term matches this definition? “the dominant division of gymnosperms with the most variety of species”
why: conifer: the dominant division of gymnosperms with the most variety of species

q: Which term matches this definition? “a division of gymnosperms that grow in tropical climates and resemble palm trees”
why: cycad: a division of gymnosperms that grow in tropical climates and resemble palm trees

q: Which term matches this definition? “a division of gymnosperm with one living species, the Gingko biloba, a tree with fan-shaped leaves”
why: gingkophyte: a division of gymnosperm with one living species, the Gingko biloba, a tree with fan-shaped leaves

q: Which term matches this definition? “a division of gymnosperms with varied morphological features that produce vessel elements in their woody tissues”
why: gnetophyte: a division of gymnosperms with varied morphological features that produce vessel elements in their woody tissues

q: Which term matches this definition? “a seed plant with naked seeds (seeds exposed on modified leaves or in cones)”

card.q: At what stage does the diploid zygote form? 1. When the female cone begins to bud from the tree; 2. When the sperm nucleus and the egg nucleus fuse; 3. When the seeds drop from the tree; 4. When the pollen tube begins to grow
card.a: B. The diploid zygote forms after the pollen tube has finished forming so that the male generative nucleus (sperm) can fuse with the female egg.

card.q: What are the four modern-day groups of gymnosperms?
card.a: The four modern-day groups of gymnosperms are Coniferophyta, Cycadophyta, Gingkophyta, and Gnetophyta.

q: Pollen grains develop in which structure?
why: The correct answer is: the anther. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Corn develops from a seedling with a single cotyledon, displays parallel veins on its leaves, and produces monosulcate pollen. It is most likely:
why: The correct answer is: a monocot. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “a sac-like structure at the tip of the stamen in which pollen grains are produced”

q: Which term matches this definition? “the division to which angiosperms belong”
why: Anthophyta: the division to which angiosperms belong

q: Which term matches this definition? “a group of plants that probably branched off before the separation of monocots and eudicots”

q: Which term matches this definition? “the female reproductive part of a flower consisting of the stigma, style, and ovary”

q: Which term matches this definition? “the collection of petals”

q: Which term matches this definition? “the one (monocot) or two (dicot) primitive leaves present in a seed”

card.q: If a flower lacked a megasporangium, what type of gamete would it not be able to form? If it lacked a microsporangium, what type of gamete would not form?
card.a: Without a megasporangium, an egg would not form; without a microsporangium, pollen would not form.

card.q: Cycads are considered endangered species and their trade is severely restricted. Customs officials stop suspected smugglers, who claim that the plants in their possession are palm trees and not cycads. How would a botanist distinguish between the two types of plants?
card.a: The resemblance between cycads and palm trees is only superficial. Cycads are gymnosperms and do not bear flowers or fruit. Unlike palms, cycads produce cones; large, female cones that produce naked seeds, and smaller male cones on separate plants.

card.q: What are the two structures that allow angiosperms to be the dominant form of plant life in most terrestrial ecosystems?
card.a: Angiosperms are successful because of flowers and fruit. These structures protect reproduction from variability in the environment.

q: Which of the following is not a feature common to most animals?
options: development into a fixed body plan
why: The correct answer is: asexual reproduction. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which of the following does not occur?
why: The correct answer is: diploblastic eucoelomate. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

q: Which term matches this definition? “having no plane of symmetry”
why: asymmetrical: having no plane of symmetry

q: Which term matches this definition? “describing an animal in which the blastopore develops into the anus, with the second opening developing into the mouth”
why: deuterostome: describing an animal in which the blastopore develops into the anus, with the second opening developing into the mouth

card.q: How are specialized tissues important for animal function and complexity?
card.a: Specialized tissues allow more efficient functioning because differentiated tissue types can perform unique functions and work together in tandem to allow the animal to perform more functions. For example, specialized muscle tissue allows directed and efficient movement, and specialized nervous tissue allows for multiple sensory modalities as well as the ability to respond to various sensory information; these functions are not necessarily available to other non-animal organisms.

card.q: Using the following terms, explain what classifications and groups humans fall into, from the most general to the most specific: symmetry, germ layers, coelom, embryological development.
card.a: Humans have body plans that are bilaterally symmetrical and are characterized by the development of three germ layers, making them triploblasts. Humans have true coeloms, and are thus eucoelomates. Humans are deuterostomes.

q: Cubozoans are ________.

card.q: Describe the feeding mechanism of sponges and identify how it is different from other animals.
card.a: The sponges draw water carrying food particles into the spongocoel using the beating of flagella in the choanocytes. The food particles are caught by the collar of the choanocyte and brought into the cell by phagocytosis. Digestion of the food particle takes place inside the cell. The difference between this and the mechanisms of other animals is that digestion takes place within cells rather than outside of cells. It means that the organism can feed only on particles smaller than the cells themselves.

card.q: Compare the structural differences between Porifera and Cnidaria.
card.a: Poriferans do not possess true tissues, whereas cnidarians do have tissues. Because of this difference, poriferans do not have a nerve net or muscle cells for locomotion, which cnidarians have.

q: Which group of flatworms are primarily external parasites of fish?
why: The correct answer is: monogeneans. Re-read the lesson above to see why.

why: dioecious: having separate male and female sexes

card.q: Speculate as to what advantage(s) a complete digestive system has over an incomplete digestive system?
card.a: In a complete digestive system, food material is not mixed with waste material, so the digestion and uptake of nutrients can be more efficient. In addition, the complete digestive system allows for an orderly progression of digestion of food matter and the specialization of different zones of the digestive tract.

card.q: Describe a potential advantage and disadvantage of the cuticle of ecdysozoans.
card.a: An advantage is that it is a tough covering that is protective against adverse environments, and predators and parasites. A disadvantage is that it must be shed and regrown for the animal to grow, which requires energy and makes the animal vulnerable during this process.

card.q: Describe the morphology and anatomy of mollusks.
card.a: Mollusks have a large muscular foot that may be modified in various ways, such as into tentacles, but it functions in locomotion. They have a mantle, a structure of tissue that covers and encloses the dorsal portion of the animal and secretes the shell when it is present. The mantle encloses the mantle cavity, which houses the gills (when present), excretory pores, anus, and gonadopores. The coelom of mollusks is restricted to the region around the systemic heart. The main body cavity is a hemocoel. Many mollusks have a radula near the mouth that is used for scraping food.

q: The circulatory fluid in echinoderms is _____.

q: Which of the following is not a member of the phylum Chordata?

why: Chordata: a phylum of animals distinguished by their possession of a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, and a post-anal tail at some point during their development

card.q: Sessile adult tunicates lose the notochord; what does this suggest about one function of this structure?
card.a: It suggests that the notochord is important for support during locomotion of an organism.

card.q: During embryonic development, what features do we share with tunicates or lancelets?
card.a: During embryonic development, we also have a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve tube, pharyngeal slits, and a post-anal tail.

card.q: What can be inferred about the evolution of the cranium and the vertebral column from examining hagfishes and lampreys?
card.a: Comparison of hagfishes with lampreys shows that the cranium evolved first in early vertebrates, as it is seen in hagfishes, which evolved earlier than lampreys. This was followed by evolution of the vertebral column, a primitive form of which is seen in lampreys and not in hagfishes.

card.q: Explain why frogs are restricted to a moist environment.
card.a: A moist environment is required as frog eggs lack a shell and dehydrate quickly in dry environments.

card.q: Describe three adaptations that allow for flight in birds.
card.a: Birds have feathers that streamline the bird body and assist in flight. They also have pneumatic bones that are hollow rather than tissue-filled. Birds are endothermic, which allows for a higher metabolism demanded by flight.

card.q: When bacteria are destroyed by leukocytes, pyrogens are released into the blood. Pyrogens reset the body’s thermostat to a higher temperature, resulting in fever. How might pyrogens cause the body temperature to rise?
card.a: Pyrogens increase body temperature by causing the blood vessels to constrict, inducing shivering, and stopping sweat glands from secreting fluid.

card.q: Describe how the body’s mechanisms maintain homeostasis?
card.a: The body has a sensor that detects a deviation of the state of the cells or the body from the set point. The information is relayed to a control center, usually the brain, where signals go to effectors. Those effectors cause a negative feedback response that moves the state of the body in a direction back toward the set point.

card.q: Why is excretion important in order to achieve osmotic balance?
card.a: Excretion allows an organism to rid itself of waste molecules that could be toxic if allowed to accumulate. It also allows the organism to keep the amount of water and dissolved solutes in balance.

card.q: What is the role of the accessory organs in digestion?
card.a: Accessory organs play an important role in producing and delivering digestive juices to the intestine during digestion and absorption. Specifically, the salivary glands, liver, pancreas, and gallbladder play important roles. Malfunction of any of these organs can lead to disease states.

card.q: What is the role of minerals in maintaining good health?
card.a: Minerals—such as potassium, sodium, and calcium—are required for the functioning of many cellular processes. While minerals are required in trace amounts, not having minerals in the diet can be potentially harmful.

card.q: Discuss why obesity is a growing epidemic.
card.a: In the United States, obesity, particularly childhood obesity, is a growing concern. Some of the contributors to this situation include sedentary lifestyles and consuming more processed foods and less fruits and vegetables. As a result, even young children who are obese can face health concerns.

card.q: Describe the function of these terms and describe where they are located: main bronchus, trachea, alveoli.
card.a: The main bronchus is the conduit in the lung that funnels air to the airways where gas exchange occurs. The main bronchus attaches the lungs to the very end of the trachea where it bifurcates. The trachea is the cartilaginous structure that extends from the pharynx to the lungs. It serves to funnel air to the lungs. The alveoli are the site of gas exchange; they are located at the terminal regions of the lung and are attached to the alveolar sacs, which come from the alveolar ducts and respiratory bronchioles terminal bronchi.

card.q: How does the structure of alveoli maximize gas exchange?
card.a: The sac-like structure of the alveoli increases their surface area. In addition, the alveoli are made of thin-walled cells. These features allows gases to easily diffuse across the cells.

card.q: Describe the cardiac cycle.
card.a: The heart receives an electrical signal triggering the cardiac muscle cells in the atria to contract. The signal pauses before passing onto the ventricles so the blood is pumped through the body. This is the systolic phase. The heart then relaxes in diastole and fills again with blood.

card.q: What is a similarity and a difference between an exocrine gland and an endocrine gland?
card.a: The cells of both exocrine and endocrine glands produce a product that will be secreted by the gland. An exocrine gland has a duct and secretes its product to the outside of the gland, not into the bloodstream. An endocrine gland secretes its product into the bloodstream and does not use a duct.

card.q: Describe how hormone receptors can play a role in affecting the size of the responses of tissues to hormones.
card.a: The number of receptors that respond to a hormone can change, resulting in increased or decreased cell sensitivity. The number of receptors can increase in response to rising hormone levels, called up-regulation, making the cell more sensitive to the hormone and allowing for more cellular activity. The number of receptors can also decrease in response to rising hormone levels, called down-regulation, leading to reduced cellular activity.

card.q: Many hormone systems regulate body functions through opposing hormone actions. Describe how opposing hormone actions regulate blood-glucose levels?
card.a: Blood-glucose levels are regulated by hormones produced by the pancreas: insulin and glucagon. When blood-glucose levels are increasing, the pancreas releases insulin, which stimulates uptake of glucose by cells. When blood-glucose levels are decreasing, the pancreas releases glucagon, which stimulates the release of stored glucose by the liver to the bloodstream.

card.q: How are neurons similar to other cells? How are they unique?
card.a: Neurons contain organelles common to all cells, such as a nucleus and mitochondria. They are unique because they contain dendrites, which can receive signals from other neurons, and axons that can send these signals to other cells.

card.q: What are the main functions of the spinal cord?
card.a: The spinal cord transmits sensory information from the body to the brain and motor commands from the brain to the body through its connections with peripheral nerves. It also controls motor reflexes.

card.q: What are the main differences between the sympathetic and parasympathetic branches of the autonomic nervous system?
card.a: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for “fight or flight,” whereas the parasympathetic nervous system allows the body to “rest and digest.” Sympathetic neurons release norepinephrine onto target organs; parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine. Sympathetic neuron cell bodies are located in sympathetic ganglia. Parasympathetic neuron cell bodies are located in the brainstem and sacral spinal cord. Activation of the sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate and blood pressure and decreases digestion and blood flow to the skin. Activation of the parasympathetic nervous system decreases heart rate and blood pressure and increases digestion and blood flow to the skin.

card.q: What are the main functions of the sensory-somatic nervous system?
card.a: The sensory-somatic nervous system transmits sensory information from the skin, muscles, and sensory organs to the CNS. It also sends motor commands from the CNS to the muscles, causing them to contract.

card.q: Influenza virus is packaged in a viral envelope, which fuses with the plasma membrane. This way, the virus can exit the host cell without killing it. What advantage does the virus gain by keeping the host cell alive?

card.q: Why can’t dogs catch the measles?
card.a: The virus cannot attach to dog cells because dog cells do not express the receptors for the virus or there is no cell within the dog that is permissive for viral replication.

card.q: Why is immunization after being bitten by a rabid animal so effective?
card.a: Rabies vaccine works after a bite because it takes two weeks for the virus to travel from the site of the bite to the central nervous system, where the most severe symptoms of the disease occur. The vaccine is able to cause an immune response in the body during this time that clears the infection before it reaches the nervous system.

card.q: Different MHC class I molecules between donor and recipient cells can lead to rejection of a transplanted organ or tissue. Suggest a reason for this.

card.q: If a series of genetic mutations prevented some, but not all, of the complement proteins from binding antibodies or pathogens, would the entire complement system be compromised?

Because the complement involves the binding of activated proteins in a specific sequence, when one or more proteins in the sequence is absent, the subsequent proteins would be incapable of binding to elicit the complement’s pathogen-destructive effects.

card.q: The Rh antigen is found on Rh-positive red blood cells. An Rh-negative person can usually carry an Rh-positive fetus to term without difficulty. However, having a second Rh-positive fetus may launch an immune attack that causes hemolytic disease of the newborn. Why do you think hemolytic disease is only a problem during the second or subsequent pregnancies?
card.a: If the blood of the mother and fetus mixes, memory cells that recognize the Rh antigen of the fetus can form in the mother late in the first pregnancy. During subsequent pregnancies, these memory cells launch an immune attack on the fetal blood cells of an Rh-positive fetus. Injection of anti-Rh antibody during the first pregnancy prevents the immune response from occurring.

card.q: How do B and T cells differ with respect to antigens that they bind?
card.a: T cells bind antigens that have been digested and embedded in MHC molecules by APCs. In contrast, B cells function as APCs to bind intact, unprocessed antigens.

card.q: Why is the immune response after reinfection much faster than the adaptive immune response after the initial infection?
card.a: Upon reinfection, the memory cells will immediately differentiate into plasma cells and CTLs without input from APCs or T_H cells. In contrast, the adaptive immune response to the initial infection requires time for naïve B and T cells with the appropriate antigen specificities to be identified and activated.

card.q: Compared to separate sexes and assuming self-fertilizing is not possible, what might be one advantage and one disadvantage to hermaphroditism?
card.a: A possible advantage of hermaphroditism might be that anytime an individual of the same species is encountered a mating is possible, unlike separate sexes that must find an individual of the right sex to mate. (Also, every individual in a hermaphrodite population is able to produce offspring, which is not the case in populations with separate sexes.) A disadvantage might be that hermaphrodite populations are less efficient because they do not specialize in one sex or another, which means a hermaphrodite does not produce as many offspring through eggs or sperm as do species with separate sexes. (Other answers are possible.)

card.q: Compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis as to timing of the processes, and the number and type of cells finally produced.
card.a: Stem cells are laid down in the male during gestation and lie dormant until adolescence. Stem cells in the female increase to one to two million and enter the first meiotic division and are arrested in prophase. At adolescence, spermatogenesis begins and continues until death, producing the maximum number of sperm with each meiotic division. Oogenesis continues again at adolescence in batches of eggs with each menstrual cycle. These primary oocytes finish the first meiotic division, producing a viable egg with most of the cytoplasm and its contents, and a second cell called a polar body containing 23 chromosomes. The second meiotic division is initiated and arrested in metaphase. At ovulation, one egg is released. If this egg is fertilized, it finishes the second meiotic division. This is a diploid, fertilized egg.

card.q: Describe the events in the ovarian cycle leading up to ovulation.
card.a: Low levels of progesterone allow the hypothalamus to send GnRH to the anterior pituitary and cause the release of FSH and LH. FSH stimulates follicles on the ovary to grow and prepare the eggs for ovulation. As the follicles increase in size, they begin to release estrogen and a low level of progesterone into the blood. The level of estrogen rises to a peak, causing a spike in the concentration of LH. This causes the most mature follicle to rupture and ovulation occurs.

card.q: Describe the stages of labor.
card.a: Stage one of labor results in uterine contractions, which thin the cervix and dilate the cervical opening. Stage two delivers the baby, and stage three delivers the placenta.

card.q: Describe the growth at various parts of the S-shaped curve of logistic growth.
card.a: In the first part of the curve, when few individuals of the species are present and resources are plentiful, growth is exponential, similar to a J-shaped curve. Later, growth slows due to the species using up resources. Finally, the population levels off at the carrying capacity of the environment, and it is relatively stable over time.

card.q: Give an example of how density-dependent and density-independent factors might interact.
card.a: If a natural disaster such as a fire happened in the winter, when populations are low, it would have a greater effect on the overall population and its recovery than if the same disaster occurred during the summer, when population levels are high.

On the other hand, a high proportion of older individuals is seen mostly in countries with zero growth, and a low proportion is most common in rapidly growing countries.

card.q: Describe the competitive exclusion principle and its effects on competing species.
card.a: The competitive exclusion principles states that no two species competing for the same resources at the same time and place can co-exist over time. Thus, one of the competing species will eventually dominate. On the other hand, if the species evolve such that they use resources from different parts of the habitat or at different times of day, the two species can exist together indefinitely.

card.q: Describe the potential effects when a keystone species is removed from a community.
card.a: Removing a keystone species will have dramatic effects on the abundance of individuals in other populations, increasing some and decreasing others. This affects the interactions between populations such as competition and predator-prey relationships. In addition, the community may show a loss of diversity.

card.q: Compare grazing and detrital food webs. Why would they both be present in the same ecosystem?
card.a: Grazing food webs have a producer at their base, which is either a plant for terrestrial ecosystems or a phytoplankton for aquatic ecosystems. The producers pass their energy to the various trophic levels of consumers. At the base of detrital food webs are the decomposers, which pass their energy to a variety of other consumers. Detrital food webs are important for the health of many grazing food webs because they eliminate dead and decaying organic material, thus clearing space for new organisms and removing potential causes of disease.

card.q: Why are drinking water supplies still a major concern for many countries?
card.a: Most of the water on Earth is salt water, which humans cannot drink unless the salt is removed. Some fresh water is locked in glaciers and polar ice caps, or is present in the atmosphere. The earth’s water supplies are threatened by pollution and exhaustion. The effort to supply fresh drinking water to the planet’s ever-expanding human population is seen as a major challenge in this century.

card.q: The extremely low precipitation of subtropical desert biomes might lead one to expect fire to be a major disturbance factor; however, fire is more common in the temperate grassland biome than in the subtropical desert biome. Why is this?
card.a: Fire is less common in desert biomes than in temperate grasslands because deserts have low net primary productivity, thus very little plant biomass to fuel a fire.

card.q: In what ways are the subtropical desert and the Arctic tundra similar?
card.a: Both the subtropical desert and the Arctic tundra have a low supply of water. In the desert, this is due to extremely low precipitation, and in the Arctic tundra, much of the water is unavailable to plants because it is frozen. Both the subtropical desert and the Arctic tundra have low net primary productivity.

card.q: Describe the conditions and challenges facing organisms living in the intertidal zone.
card.a: Organisms living in the intertidal zone must tolerate periodic exposure to air and sunlight and must be able to be periodically dry. They also must be able to endure the pounding waves; for this reason, some shoreline organisms have hard exoskeletons that provide protection while also reducing the likelihood of drying out.

card.q: Explain how biodiversity loss can impact crop diversity.
card.a: Crop plants are derived from wild plants, and genes from wild relatives are frequently brought into crop varieties by plant breeders to add valued characteristics to the crops. If the wild species are lost, then this genetic variation would no longer be available.

card.q: Describe the mechanisms by which human population growth and resource use causes increased extinction rates.

card.q: Explain what extinction threats a frog living on a mountainside in Costa Rica might face.
card.a: The frog is at risk from global warming shifting its preferred habitat up the mountain. In addition, it will be at risk from exotic species, either as a new predator or through the impact of transmitted diseases such as chytridiomycosis. It is also possible that habitat destruction will threaten the species.

card.q: Describe two considerations in conservation preserve design.
card.a: Larger preserves will contain more species. Preserves should have a buffer around them to protect species from edge effects. Preserves that are round or square are better than preserves with many thin arms.

card.q: Describe what happens to an ecosystem when a keystone species is removed.
